{{< include _compose-kit.qmd >}}

Arranging means taking music that already exists, a melody with its chords, and deciding **who plays what**. The band version of this question is in
[Arranging 1](arrange-band.qmd). This lesson asks it for orchestral instruments, starting with the smallest orchestral group that
can do everything: the **string quartet** (two violins, viola, cello).

**How to use the page.** ▶ plays each example on the piano (the site has no string samples), so listen for the **parts**:
which line moves, which holds, which is on top. Then find a recording of a real quartet and listen for the same things.

## 1. Four jobs

Almost every arrangement gives out the same four jobs:

| Job | What it does | Usually given to |
|---|---|---|
| **Melody** | the tune: what the listener follows | the highest part, or the instrument with the strongest sound in that register |
| **Bass** | the lowest note of each chord, which tells the ear what the harmony is | cello, double bass, bassoon, tuba |
| **Harmony** | the rest of the chord, filling the middle | inner parts: second violin, viola, horns, clarinets |
| **Countermelody** | a second tune that moves when the melody holds still | a contrasting instrument in a different register |

Not every job is needed all the time. Taking one away (no bass, or melody alone) is one of the strongest effects an arranger has.

## 2. The same melody, two ways

The melody is the period from [Composing 1](compose-melody.qmd#the-period). First as a **chorale**: the melody on top, the other three
parts holding the chords. The texture is called **homophonic**: one tune, with chords moving in the same rhythm or slower.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="96" data-width="680"><script type="text/plain">

T:String quartet 1: melody and held chords
M:4/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=96
K:C
%%score [1 2 3 4]
V:1 name="Violin I" clef=treble
V:2 name="Violin II" clef=treble
V:3 name="Viola" clef=alto
V:4 name="Cello" clef=bass
[V:1] E2 G2 c2 G2 | A2 F2 G4 | A2 c2 G2 E2 | D6 z2 | E2 G2 c2 G2 | A2 F2 G4 | A2 F2 D2 B,2 | C6 z2 |]
[V:2] C8 | C4 C4 | C4 C4 | B,8 | C8 | C4 C4 | C4 B,4 | C6 z2 |]
[V:3] G,8 | A,4 G,4 | A,4 G,4 | G,8 | G,8 | A,4 G,4 | A,4 F,4 | E,6 z2 |]
[V:4] C,8 | F,4 C,4 | F,4 C,4 | G,,8 | C,8 | F,4 C,4 | F,4 G,,4 | C,6 z2 |]
</script></div>

Now with a **countermelody** in the second violin (it moves when the melody holds a long note, in bars 2, 4 and 6) and a bass that walks
in quarter notes. The viola rests. Three lines that each have their own shape make a busier, more **polyphonic** texture.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="96" data-width="680"><script type="text/plain">

V:3 name="Cello" clef=bass

[V:2] C4 E4 | C4 E2 D2 | F4 C4 | G,2 B,2 D2 B,2 | C4 E4 | C4 E2 D2 | C4 G,4 | G,6 z2 |]
[V:3] C,2 E,2 G,2 E,2 | F,2 A,2 C,2 E,2 | F,2 A,2 C,2 E,2 | G,,4 D,4 | C,2 E,2 G,2 E,2 | F,2 A,2 C,2 E,2 | F,2 A,2 G,2 F,2 | C,6 z2 |]
</script></div>

Neither is better. The first is calm and warm; the second has more going on, and the melody has to work harder to be heard. Choosing
between them depends on what you want the listener to feel. Write that reason down: it is your **artistic choice**, and explaining it is
half of MYP Criterion B (see [Process 2](process-crit-b.qmd)).

## 3. Techniques

**Doubling.** Two instruments play the same line, at the same pitch (unison) or an octave apart. Unison makes a new blended colour (flute and
violin together sound like neither). Octaves make a line stronger and easier to hear. Doubling the melody is the simplest way to bring it out.

**Spacing.** Leave wide gaps between the low notes and put the close intervals at the top, the way the harmonic series does (see
[Sound 1](sound-harmonics.qmd)). Close chords low down sound muddy. In the first quartet, the cello sits an octave or more below the viola.

**Passing the tune around.** Give the melody to a different instrument when it repeats: violin first, then cello an octave lower, then the
clarinet. The listener hears the same tune in a new colour, and the players get a turn each.

**Balance.** A melody in the middle of the texture is easily covered. Make the accompaniment quieter (mark it *p* when the melody is *mf*),
thinner (fewer notes), or further away in register.

**Rests.** Wind and brass players have to breathe, and every player needs to rest their lip, arm or hands. A part that plays every bar is tiring
to play and to hear. Silence also makes an instrument's return noticeable.

**Write for the instrument.** Check every part against the ranges in [Composing 4](compose-instruments.qmd), and write transposing parts in
the player's key. The [transposer there](compose-instruments.qmd#try-it-the-transposer) does both.

## 4. Hear the principle: melody

Nikolay Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration by showing **real orchestral bars** from his own operas and symphonic works, grouped by the
question each one answers. The site has those bars as full scores. Each link below opens one **in the full-score player**: it plays on the
band's samples, and you can **tick instruments off and on** (or pick a view by family) to hear what each doubling adds. The advice is his,
retold here in the site's words; the examples are his (see Works Cited). The book's captions give no bar numbers, so each link says how many
bars the example has.

**How to listen.** Play the example with everything on. Then switch off the doubling instrument, so only the main line is left, and play it again.
Say what the doubling changed: louder, fuller, warmer, brighter, or harder to hear.

### A melody has to stand out

Whatever it is made of, the tune must be set *in relief* against its accompaniment. That can be done with dynamics alone, with colour (a timbre
that contrasts with the accompaniment) and with **weight** (doubling the line). A tune in the top or bottom register stands out by its position;
a tune in the middle of the orchestra needs help from the other tools.

### Strings: one section, or one section doubling another

- **A string instrument alone.** Violins sing the tune in the soprano range; violas suit shorter, characterful phrases (their tone is slightly
  nasal); cellos are the choice for intense, warm tunes on their top string; basses only in unison or octaves with the cellos.
  Hear it: [violins, Sheherazade, 26 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-001), [violas, Pan Voyevoda, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-004), [double bass doubled by bassoons, Kitesh, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-010).
- **In unison.** Both violin sections together add power and richness without changing the colour ([strings only, Sheherazade, 21 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-012)).
  Adding cellos to violins or violas gives a fuller sound where the **cello colour wins** ([violins + cellos + English horn, Snegourotchka, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-017)).
  Violins, violas and cellos all in unison only work in the middle register, strong when loud and rich when quiet ([Sheherazade, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-019)).
  Cellos with basses give a heavy low line ([Kitesh, 4 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-021)).
- **In octaves.** The most common way to reinforce a string tune. Violins in octaves with each other suit very high notes ([Tsar Saltan, 4 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-023));
  violins with violas keep the lower octave below the violin's open G ([Sadko, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-027), [Snegourotchka, 11 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-028)); violins with cellos make a
  very expressive, resonant cantabile ([Antar, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-029)); violas with basses is rare ([Kitesh, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-031)). A tune pitched very high is usually
  doubled an octave *below*, one pitched very low an octave *above*.
- **Two octaves, thirds and sixths.** Two doublings for a tense full tune ([Antar, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-032), [Snegourotchka, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-033)); thirds, with the same
  kind of tone in both lines ([Kitesh, 10 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-034)); sixths, where different colours are fine ([Spanish Capriccio, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-035)).

### Woodwind: solos, then combinations

- **Each wind alone** has its own colour, described in [Composing 4](compose-instruments.qmd): [piccolo, 16 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-036), [flute, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-038),
  [oboe, 12 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-041), [English horn, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-044), [small clarinet, 11 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-046), [bass clarinet, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-047), [bassoon, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-049).
- **Two colours in unison** make a third colour, fuller than either, and each wind leads in the register where it is strongest: flute + oboe
  ([Snegourotchka, 10 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-052)), flute + clarinet ([Kitesh, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-053)), oboe + clarinet ([Snegourotchka, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-054)), all four ([Snegourotchka, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-055)).
  The price is variety: blended timbres lose some of their own character, so do not blend everything.
- **In octaves**, keep the winds in their normal score order (flutes above oboes above clarinets above bassoons); flipping the order muddles the registers.
  Different colours work well ([flute + oboe, 2 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-056), [flute + English horn, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-057), [clarinet + bassoon, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-059)); two of the *same* wind in
  octaves is weaker unless the strings help. Pairs from one family are safe: piccolo + small clarinet ([Mlada, 26 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-061)).
- **Three and four octaves** spread one tune over the whole wind section ([Antar, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-065), [Sheherazade, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-066)).
- **Thirds and sixths.** Use two instruments of one kind for thirds, different kinds for sixths, and keep the natural register order
  ([Spanish Capriccio, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-067), [Christmas Night, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-068), [mixed thirds and sixths, Kitesh, 4 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-069)).

### Brass

Brass tunes are best when simple, diatonic and strong: fanfares and calls ([Kitesh, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-070), [trumpet, Sadko, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-071)), triumphant or sombre
melodies ([Snegourotchka, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-072)), and the warmer horn in quiet passages ([Antar, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-073)). Chromatic, passionate tunes suit brass less
([Sheherazade, 3 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-074)). Brass of one kind blends well in unison, octaves, thirds and sixths ([horns, May Night, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-076), [octaves, Snegourotchka, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-095)).

### Combining the groups

- **Strings + wind** always blend: the wind adds weight and the strings soften the wind. Match registers (violins with flute, oboe or clarinet; violas
  with oboe, English horn, clarinet or bassoon; cellos with clarinet or bassoon). Hear it: [violas + clarinet, May Night, 4 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-080),
  [violins + oboe, Sadko, 13 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-081), [violas + English horn, Sadko, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-082); in octaves [Ivan the Terrible, 15 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-085), [Sadko, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-086).
- **Strings + brass** never blend as smoothly; horns with cellos are the best pair, and cellos + basses with trombones + tuba make a massive low line ([Golden Cockerel, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-092)).
- **All three groups** together give a full, even sound whose character depends on how many of each ([violins + clarinet + horn, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-093) and
  [the same with a trumpet, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-094), both Snegourotchka).

**Try it.** Take two melody examples (for instance [strings in octaves](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-023) and [flute + oboe in unison](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-052)). For each, write what the doubling does to
(a) loudness, (b) colour and (c) how easily you can follow the tune. Then use one of the techniques on your own melody in the arrangement below.

## 5. Hear the principle: harmony

The same book turns from tunes to **chords**: how many parts, how to space them, and how each group handles them. As above, each link is a real
example in the player, and you can switch instruments off and on.

### Number of parts and doubling

Nearly all orchestral harmony is four-part, even when it sounds like six or eight, because the extra instruments are *doubling* four underlying
lines. So decide the four lines first, then spread them across instruments. In widely spaced chords only the top two lines are usually doubled in
octaves; doubling the bass makes a chord heavy, and doubling the tenor fills the middle and turns the spacing close. (The book makes these points
with its own small good / bad figures, which are not numbered examples; the links below are real passages that show the habits at work.)

### Distribution: wide at the bottom, close at the top

Space a chord the way the harmonic series does (see [Sound 1](sound-harmonics.qmd)): big gaps low, small gaps high. The bass should rarely sit more
than an octave from the part above it, and the middle should have no hole in it, least of all in loud passages.
Hear it in strings: [Snegourotchka, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-097), [Tsar Saltan, 15 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-098), [Snegourotchka, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-099), [Christmas Night, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-100).

### String harmony

Strings give the most even chords when each line has its own section: a sustained or tremolo chord can put divided violins and violas on top of
undivided cellos and basses, with the low strings kept lighter so they do not weigh the chord down ([Christmas Night, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-101),
[Snegourotchka, 10 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-102), [Golden Cockerel, 4 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-104)). Short chords on strings work when loud and sharp, ideally with winds supporting them ([Sheherazade, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-019)).

### Woodwind harmony

The book's habits for wind chords: keep the same instruments doubled (or not doubled) through a passage; keep the normal order of register unless
you cross or enclose parts on purpose; put instruments of similar register together (a weak low flute under piercing oboes is out of balance); and
give consonant intervals to instruments of the same kind. A wind pair can be laid out by **overlaying** (strict register order), **crossing** or
**enclosing** one colour between two others. Hear woodwind chords: [flute, clarinet, bassoon, violin, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-105), [Christmas Night prelude, 8 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-106),
[Snegourotchka, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-108), [Sheherazade, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-109), [Sadko, 23 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-112), [Tsar's Bride, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-113). Mixing doubled timbres (a flute
with an oboe, a clarinet with a flute) evens the sound out ([Tsar Saltan, 13 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-110), [5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-111)).

### Brass harmony

Four horns make a perfectly balanced four-part chord on their own, and brass chords, like the woodwinds', are written close with no empty spaces.
Hear brass harmony: [Sadko, 13 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-131), [Christmas Night, 6 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-132), [Kitesh, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-134), [Golden Cockerel, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-135), [Tsar Saltan, 16 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-138).

### Groups combined

When winds, brass and strings play chords together, the usual plan is to build a four-part basis and let each group take a share, or to let one group
hold the harmony while another moves. Hear it: [Tsar's Bride, 9 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-141), [Sadko, woodwind alone, 5 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-144), [Sadko, 7 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-145), [Tsar Saltan, 10 bars](/theory/analysed-scores/full-scores.html?id=rimsky-149).

**Try it.** Choose one chord example each from strings, woodwind and brass. Untick the instruments one family at a time. Which line (bass, tenor, alto,
soprano) does each group give up when it is gone? Then write a four-part progression and give it first to strings, then to woodwind, and describe the
difference in a sentence each.

## 6. Arrange a melody

Take a melody you know or have written: eight or sixteen bars with chords. Arrange it for the instruments your class has.

1. List your players, their instruments and their ranges.
2. Decide the four jobs for each section of the melody. **Change something when the melody repeats.**
3. Write it in the [Notation page](/tools/notation.qmd) or a notation program. Check the ranges, transpose the parts.
4. Have the players play it, or play it back. **Record it.** Write down what didn't work (a covered melody, a part too high, a muddy chord)
   and what you changed.
5. Keep the first version and the last version. The differences, and your reasons for them, are what your process journal shows.
